report:
Based on this research, "no" is a reasonable but nuanced answer—dexamethasone reduces mortality risk on a population level, but it does not "ensure" survival for individual critically ill patients, and benefit is not universal.

**Report:**

Corticosteroids like dexamethasone reduce the *probability* of death from severe COVID-19, but they do not "ensure" survival — many treated patients still die, and benefit is not universal across all patients.

The landmark UK RECOVERY trial (NEJM, 2020) found dexamethasone (6 mg/day, 10 days) lowered 28-day mortality among hospitalized COVID-19 patients requiring oxygen or ventilation — from about 40% to 29% in ventilated patients, and from 25% to 22% in those needing supplemental oxygen. This is a substantial relative reduction (roughly one-third and one-fifth respectively) but still leaves a large share of critically ill patients dying despite treatment (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2021436).

The WHO-led prospective meta-analysis (JAMA, 2020), pooling seven randomized trials of corticosteroids in critically ill COVID-19 patients, similarly found lower 28-day mortality with corticosteroids (32% vs. 40% with usual care/placebo) — an important, statistically significant benefit, but again not a guarantee of survival; roughly one-third of steroid-treated critically ill patients still died (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2770279).

Notably, RECOVERY found no benefit — and possible harm — in patients not requiring oxygen support, showing the effect is context-dependent, not universal.

**Conclusion:** The evidence confirms your intuition: dexamethasone and similar corticosteroids improve survival odds for critically ill, oxygen-dependent COVID-19 patients at a population level, but they do not guarantee survival for any individual patient — substantial mortality persists even with treatment, and steroids don't help (and may harm) less severely ill patients.
